# 6. TB research and innovation

_Draft! Prepared `r Sys.time()` _

One of the three pillars of the WHO End TB Strategy, adopted by all Member States in 2014, is research and innovation (`r ref_lnk("1, 2")`). The strategy’s targets for reductions in tuberculosis (TB) disease burden set for 2035 (a 90% reduction in the TB incidence rate and a 95% reduction in the number of deaths caused by TB, compared with levels in 2015) can only be achieved with substantial technological breakthroughs, such as the availability and widespread use of a new TB vaccine (`r ref_lnk("3")`).

Since the adoption of the Strategy, Member States have reaffirmed and strengthened their commitments to TB research and innovation: in particular, through the Moscow Declaration to End TB in 2017 (`r ref_lnk("4")`), the Global Strategy for TB Research and Innovation in 2020 (`r ref_lnk("5")`) and political declarations from the United Nations (UN) high-level meetings on TB held in 2018 and 2023 (`r ref_lnk("6, 7")`). These have all emphasized the need for strengthened TB research efforts and associated increases in investment. Top priorities include: the development of more accurate and affordable rapid point-of-care tests for diagnosing TB infection and disease and for detecting drug resistance; shorter, safer regimens for treating TB infection and TB disease, especially drug-resistant TB; a TB vaccine that is effective before and after exposure across a range of age groups; and strategies to optimally scale-up effective interventions.

WHO has promoted and monitored the development of new TB diagnostics, drugs, and vaccines, as well as operational research projects, for many years. Since 2023, this has been done through a <a href="https://tbtrialtrack.who.int/#/" target="_blank">TB research tracker</a> (`r ref_lnk("8")`), regular assessments of the diagnostic landscape and, since 2026, a new WHO forum for evidence related to TB diagnostics.

A summary of the latest status of progress is provided below. This covers funding for TB research; an overview of the clinical development pipelines for new TB diagnostics, drugs, treatment regimens and vaccines as of August `r report_year`; and recent WHO initiatives to promote research and innovation, in line with the third pillar of the End TB Strategy.


## Funding for TB research

The 2023 political declaration of the UN high-level meeting on TB set an ambitious target to mobilize US$ 5 billion annually for TB research by 2027. The most recent data show that only US$ 1.2 billion was available in 2023 (`r ref_lnk("9")`), a modest increase compared with approximately US$ 1 billion in 2022 and  far short of what is required (`r lnk("Fig. 6.1")`). Updated data are expected to become available in December 2026.

### `r anch("Fig. 6.1")` <span class="red">Fig. 6.1</span> Funding for TB research, 2015&#8211;2023
<div class="subhead">The <span class="red">red</span> line shows the target of US\$&nbsp;5 billion per year by 2027 that was set at the UN high-level meeting on TB in 2023.</div>

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, paged.print=FALSE,  fig.align = "left", fig.width=12}

# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# Create figure 6.1
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

# get the  data from here https://www.treatmentactiongroup.org/resources/tbrd-report/tbrd-report-2024/----
#  just enter it here manually

year <- c(2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023)

research <- c(0.643, 0.675, 0.639, 0.686, 0.674, 0.621, 0.726, 0.772, 0.906, 0.901, 0.915, 1.000, 1.035, 1.203)

tb_research <- data.frame(year, research)
f6.1_data <- tb_research

# Plot research funding as a simple bar chart ----

f6.1_plot <- tb_research %>%
  
  filter(year < 2024 & year >= 2015) %>%
  
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=research)) +
  
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "lightblue") +
  
  scale_x_continuous(name="", breaks = c(2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023)) +
  
  # display y-axis scale im millions
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Billions (current US$)",
                     limits = c(0,5.1)) +
  
  # add target funding of USD 5 billion as dashed horizontal line
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5,
             color = "red",
             size=1.1,
             show.legend = TRUE) +
  
  annotate("text",
           x = 2016, y = 4.8,
           label = "Target set at UN high-level meeting on TB (2023)",
           size = 4,
           color = "#222222") +
  theme_gtb()

output_ggplot(f6.1_plot, f6.1_data, show_static, pdf_csv_folder, save_csv, save_pdf)

```

<div id="fig_6_1"></div>

<div class="footnote">Source: <a href="https://www.treatmentactiongroup.org/resources/tbrd-report/tbrd-report-2024/" target="_blank">Treatment Action Group, Stop TB Partnership. Tuberculosis research funding trends 2005-2023. New York, USA 2024.</a></div>

<hr />
<br />

In 2023, drug development accounted for the largest proportion of TB research funding (35%), followed by vaccines (19%), diagnostics (14%), basic science (13%), operational research (11%) and infrastructure or unspecified research (8%). As in previous years, the public sector provided the largest share of the available funding, contributing 62% of the total, followed by philanthropic organizations (24%), the private sector (9%) and multilateral agencies (4%). The United States of America (US) National Institutes of Health (NIH) was the largest individual funder, contributing 34% of all global TB research funding in 2023 (`r ref_lnk("9")`).

The funding landscape reflects historically concentrated support among a relatively small number of major donors and research agencies.

Recent shifts in the global health landscape, including reductions in development assistance (<span class="red">Section 4.1</span>), funding uncertainty among major bilateral agencies, and growing pressure on public research budgets have raised concerns about the sustainability of TB research. Given TB research depends heavily on long-term investments, such changes can affect not only individual projects but also the broader research ecosystem, including clinical trial networks, laboratory infrastructure, surveillance systems, and research capacity in high-burden settings.

The implications of these shifts are particularly significant for low- and middle-income countries, where the burden of TB is highest and where many clinical trials and implementation studies are conducted. Funding instability and reductions may lead to delays or interruptions in research programmes, loss of skilled personnel, reduced opportunities for international collaboration, and weakened institutional capacity. These effects can slow the development and evaluation of new diagnostics, therapeutics, vaccines and strategies for TB prevention and care.

Sustained multi-year investments from public, philanthropic, private-sector, and multilateral partners remain essential. At the same time, strengthening regional research capacity, expanding South–South collaborations, fostering public–private partnerships, and aligning research priorities with national and regional needs may help reduce dependence on a limited number of funders. As the global health landscape continues to evolve, ensuring the continuity and sustainability of TB research will be critical for maintaining progress toward ending TB and advancing broader goals of global health equity and security.



## TB diagnostics

The diagnostic pipeline continues to expand. In August `r report_year`, there were 65 products for diagnosis of TB disease in development (`r lnk("Table 6.1")`). Examples of tests associated with existing classes that are in development include point-of-care urine-based lateral flow tests, near point-of-care nucleic acid amplification tests (NPOC-NAATs); low- and moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (LC-aNAATs/MC-aNAATs), low-complexity manual nucleic acid amplification tests (LC-mNAATs), line probe assays (LPAs), targeted next generation sequencing (NGS) solutions, and phenotypic broth microdilution (BMD) technologies. If approved by WHO, BMD technology will be categorized within the class of culture-based phenotypic tests. Additionally, new biomarker-based point-of-care and near point-of-care tests for TB disease are in development that could lead to the establishment of new diagnostic classes.

The pipeline also includes tests for TB infection such as interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) and TB antigen-based skin tests, as well as tools for TB screening, including computer-aided detection (CAD) solutions for digital chest radiography as well as other artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled sound analysing technologies, and biomarker-based assays with the potential to broaden current approaches to identify individuals who should be referred for further TB diagnostic testing and evaluation.

Further details, including lists of individual products, are available in a recent report (`r ref_lnk("10")`).

## Treatment for TB disease (individual drugs and regimens)

Advances in TB research are transforming treatment options, particularly for people affected by drug-resistant forms of the disease. As of August `r report_year`, the TB trials tracker indicates that there were 31 drugs for the treatment of TB disease in Phase 1, Phase 2 or Phase 3 trials, an increase from 29 in 2025 and 8 in 2015. This expanding pipeline reflects sustained investment and coordinated efforts across research platforms and consortia.

Among recent developments, interim results from the Phase 2 NC-009 trial <a href="https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06058299" target="_blank">(NCT06058299)</a>, presented at the 2025 Union World Conference on Lung Health, reported encouraging early efficacy and safety findings for TBAJ-876 (sorfequiline), in combination with pretomanid and linezolid, for people with drug-susceptible TB (`r ref_lnk("13")`). The findings support the continued clinical development of TBAJ-876-containing regimens, although full trial results have not yet been published.

The broader TB drug development pipeline encompasses both novel compounds and existing medicines being optimized for new uses. The 31 drugs comprise:

<ul>
<li>20 new chemical entities  (`r lnk("Table 6.2")`). These are alpibectir (BVL-GSK098), BTZ-043, contezolid,  delpazolid, GSK-286, ganfeborole (GSK-3036656), macozinone, MK-7762 (TBD09), quabodepistat (OPC-167832), TBAJ-587, TBAJ-876, TBD11, TBI-223, pyrifazimine (TBI-166), TBA-7371, telacebec (Q203), sanfetrinem, SQ109, sutezolid and sudapyridine (WX-081).</li> 

<li>Two drugs that received accelerated regulatory approval. These are bedaquiline and delamanid. Their efficacy as part of various treatment regimens for drug-resistant TB is currently being tested in several clinical trials, with the aim of optimizing their use and potentially expanding treatment options.</li> 

<li>One drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration under the limited population pathway for antibacterial and antifungal drugs. This is pretomanid, which is part of the 6-month regimen for MDR/RR-TB and pre-XDR-TB recommended by WHO since 2022 (`r ref_lnk("14")`). Its safety and efficacy in the treatment of drug-resistant TB continue to be tested in trials, especially in combination with bedaquiline and linezolid.</li> 

<li>Eight repurposed drugs. These are clofazimine, levofloxacin, linezolid, moxifloxacin, rifampicin (high dose), rifapentine, sitafloxacin and tedizolid. </li>
</ul>

In addition to individual drugs, various combination regimens using new or repurposed drugs, as well as host-directed therapies, are also in clinical trials or being evaluated as part of operational research projects.

## TB preventive treatment

As of August `r report_year`, at least 42 clinical trials and implementation research studies were evaluating drug regimens and delivery models for TB preventive treatment (TPT) (`r lnk("Table 6.3")`). Nine studies are assessing new TPT regimens; these include a trial investigating 4 weeks of bedaquiline for both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB in contacts and people living with HIV, a trial evaluating delamanid for the prevention of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), trials investigating short-course regimens such as thrice-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine for 1 month, and trials of rifamycin monotherapies given over 6 or 8 weeks. At least 17 studies are focused on novel TPT delivery models in community and facility-based settings, targeting children, people with HIV, and other eligible populations. Other studies are assessing the safety and efficacy of TPT in people with diabetes, pharmacokinetics and dose optimization.

## TB vaccines

As of August `r report_year`, the clinical pipelines included 17 TB vaccine candidates: 12 in active clinical development and five classified as inactive or not under active development. This is one fewer than in 2025, following discontinuation of a trial evaluating BCG vaccination to prevent infection (TIPI; NCT04453293), due to slower-than-expected recruitment and limited remaining research funding.

The inactive/not under active development category was introduced this year to distinguish candidates with no clinical development activity for 5 or more years, or whose sponsors have discontinued development, from those candidates which are in active development, consistent with the approach used by the Stop TB Partnership Working Group on New TB Vaccines.

The active pipeline comprises three Phase 1, six Phase 2 and three Phase 3 candidates (`r lnk("Table 6.4")`), including vaccines intended to prevent infection or disease and therapeutic vaccines designed to improve outcomes for people with active TB. The inactive/not under active development category includes AdHu5Ag85A, ChAdOx1 85A–MVA85A, MIP/Immuvac, VPM1002 and DAR-901; these candidates could re-enter the active pipeline if clinical development resumes. MIP/Immuvac and VPM1002 were moved to this category after Phase 3 trial results reported in 2026 did not demonstrate efficacy against the primary endpoint (`r ref_lnk("15")`). In addition, a separate Phase 3 trial failed to demonstrate the non-inferiority of VPM1002 to BCG for prevention of <i>M. tuberculosis</i> infection (`r ref_lnk("16")`). No further information is available about the future development of these candidate vaccines.

Given the high attrition rates typically associated with vaccine development, only a small proportion of early-stage candidates are expected to progress to licensure. This underscores the need for an expanded and diversified portfolio of vaccine candidates to increase the probability of success. Since the publication of the <i>Global tuberculosis report 2025</i>, WHO has led and supported several initiatives to accelerate TB vaccine development and strengthen global preparedness for the introduction of novel TB vaccines.

<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/06-11-2025-new-who-report-urges-bold-steps-for-equitable-access-to-novel-tb-vaccines" target="_blank"><b>November 2025: G20 Health Ministers’ meeting: financing and access strategies to ensure equitable introduction of novel TB vaccines</b></a> 

A WHO report calling for strengthened financing and access strategies to ensure equitable introduction of novel TB vaccines for adolescents and adults in high-burden countries was launched at a meeting of G20 health ministers in South Africa in November 2025. The report, developed through the TB Vaccine Accelerator Council’s Finance and Access Working Group (co-convened by WHO, the government of South Africa, and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance), outlines six priority actions to ensure sustainable and equitable access to TB vaccines worldwide. These include developing catalytic instruments, generating country-level evidence, mobilizing financing, strengthening supply-demand coordination, advocating for regional manufacturing in high-burden regions and promoting market transparency.</li> 

<li>

<a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/29-04-2026-global-forum-takes-stock-of-progress-on-new-tb-vaccines-for-adults-and-adolescents" target="_blank"><b>April 2026: Global TB Vaccine Accelerator Forum</b></a>

A global TB Vaccine Accelerator Forum was hosted by WHO in April 2026. This brought together governments, funders, vaccine developers, and civil society, with the aim of strengthening coordination of work related to TB vaccines. The Forum reinforced the importance of sustained readiness efforts ahead of anticipated efficacy data for novel TB vaccines in 2028, and supported continued collaboration on country preparedness, financing and delivery planning. An online community-of-practice platform for country preparedness was launched to support knowledge exchange and strengthen implementation planning for TB vaccine introduction. The platform is a collaborative effort of WHO and the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI), hosted by the online community of the Stop TB Partnership Working Group on New TB Vaccines.</li> 

<li>

<a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/20-05-2026-the-tb-vaccine-accelerator-council-meets-for-the-fourth-time" target="_blank"><b>May 2026: Fourth high-level meeting of the TB Vaccine Accelerator Council</b></a>


The TB Vaccine Accelerator Council met in May 2026 in Geneva, on the sidelines of the World Health Assembly. The Council brings together Member States and global health partners. The meeting reviewed progress on preparedness for implementation of novel TB vaccines, with a focus on strengthening domestic financing, country ownership and coordinated action to support equitable access to future TB vaccines for adolescents and adults. The Council also reviewed progress across its three working groups, including the establishment of the Working Group on Country Readiness, Advocacy and Community Partnership, efforts to expand domestic financing and regionally-diversified manufacturing of novel TB vaccines to promote long-term sustainability and equitable access, and work to evaluate the potential public health impact of new TB vaccines within an integrated approach to TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care.</li> 

<li>

<a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/23-06-2026-african-countries-convene-to-prepare-for-future-rollout-of-new-tb-vaccines-for-adults-and-adolescents" target="_blank"><b>June 2026: WHO convenes a multi-country workshop to strengthen preparedness for future rollout of new TB vaccines for adults and adolescents</b></a>

WHO convened a workshop in Nairobi, Kenya in June 2026. This brought together representatives from the Ministries of Health of Kenya, Malawi, and Zambia, along with more than 80 stakeholders—including TB survivors, civil society representatives, technical and regulatory agencies, donors, and implementing partners—with the aim of advancing country preparedness for the introduction of novel TB vaccines for adults and adolescents. The workshop aimed to catalyze early, coordinated planning to support the future rollout of these vaccines, if found safe and effective.</li>
</ul>

<script type="text/javascript">
/* JSON data objects for the figures */

var fig_6_1_data = `r tb_research %>% filter(year %in% 2015:2023) %>% toJSON("rows")`;

</script>


```{js, echo=FALSE}
/* Functions to create the figures */
function createFig_6_1() {
		$("#fig_6_1").kendoChart({
			dataSource: fig_6_1_data,
			chartArea: {
				height: 400
			},	
			legend: {
				position: "bottom"
			},
			seriesDefaults: {
				type: "column"
			},
			series: [{
				field: "research",
				color: "lightblue",
				gap: 0.1
			}],
			valueAxis: {
				labels: {
					format: "{0}"
				},
				title: {
					text: "Billions (current US$)"
				},
				line: {
					visible: false
				},
				max: 5.05,
                    line: {
                        visible: false
                    },
				plotBands: [{
					from: 4.995,
					to: 5.005,
					color: "red",
					opacity: 1,
					label: {
						text: "Target: US$ 5 billion",
						font: "20px Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif",
						position: "bottom",
						align: "center",
						padding: -25
					}
				}]
			},
			categoryAxis: {
				field: "year",
				labels: {
					rotation: "auto"
				},
				majorGridLines: {
					visible: false
				},
				plotBands: [{ 
					from: 2019, 
					to: 2021, 
					color: "grey",
					opacity: 0.5
				}]
			},
			tooltip: {
				visible: true,
				template: "TB research expenditure (#= category #): #= value # billion (current US$)"
			}
		});
}

```

```{js, echo=FALSE}
/* Create the figures after the document has been loaded */

$(document).ready(function () {
                  createFig_6_1();

}); 

```
